extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policymakers, tribunal practitioners, and public administration students
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and critical analysis of the Pension Appeals Board's organization, jurisdiction and procedures within the Canadian social security system; identifies legal, political and administrative factors that shape tribunal activity and suggests improvements. Intended to situate the PAB in context and evaluate its procedural functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative efficiency — three essential conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative efficiency is the product of three essential conditions: the possession of exact information by the decision‑making authority, speed in the formulation of the decision itself, and the existence of guarantees that decisions, once taken, will be executed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit framing in the text: efficiency depends on (1) accurate information available to decision-makers, (2) promptness in making decisions, and (3) enforceability/guarantees of execution. These three items are presented as cumulative requirements for efficient administration and serve as criteria for evaluating tribunal or administrative-body performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of individual rights — three presumptive conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Protecting the rights of individuals presupposes ... prior knowledge on the part of members of the public of their juridical situation, freedom to take part in the decision‑making process, and the existence of avenues of recourse against decisions taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three requirements constitute a normative standard for procedural fairness: (1) adequate notice/knowledge of legal status and entitlements, (2) meaningful opportunity to participate in the decision process, and (3) availability of appeals/review mechanisms. The passage presents them as necessary preconditions for safeguarding rights in administrative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and coherence of authorities, laws and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The confusion of responsibilities, the complexity of conditions of eligibility, and the poorly coordinated laws and procedures ... do little to facilitate people's access to social security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion: administrative systems should minimize fragmentation among federal/provincial/municipal agencies, simplify eligibility rules, and harmonize laws and procedures to improve public access. The text uses the government's own working paper quotation to illustrate the access costs of poor coordination—an anti-pattern to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and limits of appellate jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellate jurisdiction of the PAB does not, however, cover completely this area of administrative action. In fact, from the moment that a worker is declared self‑employed ... his claim ... no longer comes within the PAB's jurisdiction, but within that of the fiscal authorities (the Tax Review Board and the Federal Court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for tribunal design/evaluation: jurisdictional boundaries and exceptions must be explicit and well‑defined (e.g., distinctions between contributions and benefits, and special exclusions such as self‑employment). The text emphasises the need to identify which categories of decisions may be appealed to which bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency/uniformity of solutions across similar litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The similarity of the questions to be resolved and the desire for consistency in the solutions adopted are no doubt the motives that have prompted the federal legislator to place both classes of litigation before the same appeal tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative desideratum: similar fact- or law‑based disputes should be brought before a common appellate forum to promote consistent legal outcomes. This is advanced as a rationale for tribunal structure and as a metric for assessing whether organizational arrangements produce coherent jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of administrative machinery to handle volume and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The magnitude of the sums collected and the multitude of contributors ... are a sufficient indication of the size, weight and complexity of the administrative machinery needed for the work of collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: administrative institutions must be proportionately resourced and organized to manage large caseloads and complex operations (collection, control, continuing eligibility checks). The text ties observed statistics (contributions, numbers of contributors) to the requirement for adequate administrative capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistical monitoring to inform administration
rubrics_metrics.description: To enable the reader to appreciate the role played by the PAB ... it seems useful to present here some figures. ... Tables ... indicate the amounts disbursed ... and the statistical trend of the number of beneficiaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: systematic collection and analysis of statistics (contributions, benefits paid, numbers of applications and beneficiaries, litigation rates) are necessary to understand workload, identify problem areas (e.g., disability pensions lead to most litigation), and plan procedural improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of process to benefit complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: The allocation of certain types of benefits requires a relatively small number of fairly simple operations ... In other categories of benefits, however, continuous checks on the beneficiaries' right to receive them are needed, and these may require a series of operations of considerable complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design principle: administrative procedures should be calibrated to the substantive and operational complexity of the benefit category—simple, one‑off decisions for retirement/death benefits; ongoing, resource‑intensive processes for disability or conditional benefits. Use this to judge whether procedures are appropriate or overly burdensome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of decision‑making phases and pre‑appeal events
rubrics_metrics.description: In each case, it will be necessary to describe the decision‑making administrative organizations involved, the successive phases of the process and the events that may take place before decisions come before the PAB on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: procedural descriptions and evaluations should track the full chain of administrative decision‑making (actors, phases, events prior to appeal) to assess fairness, timeliness, and correctness. Transparency and documentation of those phases are presented as necessary for meaningful appellate review and for diagnosing procedural defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between efficient administrative action and safeguarding individual rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The reconciliation ... of the need for efficient administrative action with the safeguarding of the rights of individuals — the reconciliation of the primacy of the public good with a respect for legitimate private interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative standard: administrative procedure should seek an explicit balance between collective efficiency and individual protections. This balancing test functions as a high‑level criterion for assessing reforms or evaluating tribunal behaviour: neither efficiency nor rights should wholly dominate.
